I rarely quote Vladimir Putin’s moronic jokes, but here it would be quite appropriate: “If a grandmother had balls, she’d be a grandfather.” Putin isn’t getting Ukraine, period. What impact could imprisoned ultranationalist Igor Girkin's political maneuvers have on Russian President Vladimir Putin? Yesterday, the appeal court upheld the verdict of the Moscow City Court against the 53-year-old former commander of pro-Russian separatists in Donetsk Igor Girkin. Girkin (Strelkov), who is a former FSB officer, was arrested a month after the infamous Prigozhin’s coup of June 2023, and charged with “extremism”. While we know there is basically no such thing as “a former FSB officer” (you are always either an asset of the force — or a traitor, sentenced to elimination), for a long time, Girkin’s rants about the sorry state of affairs in the Russian army fighting in Ukraine didn’t cause him any trouble. So much so that most people decided that Girkin-Strelkov had powerful backers among the FSB ranks who were playing their own game. But after Prigozhin’s aborted coup, the rules of the game obviously changed. As soon as Prigozhin and his goons had been removed from the scene and their influence nullified, Girkin (who was actually a fierce opponent of Prigozhin) was arrested and thrown in Lefortovo prison — the same FSB pre-trial jail where recently arrested generals of the ministry of defence are now locked up. In January 2024, Girkin was found guilty and sentenced to 4 years in prison. Girkin’s family members were not allowed into the court during yesterday’s hearing, his wife Miroslava Reginskaya wrote on Telegram. In the near future, Girkin will be transferred to the penal colony. It was previously reported that the ex-separatist leader expressed a desire to join the Russian armed forces and go to the war in Ukraine — the war, which he personally unleashed in 2014. Under the Russian law, those convicted of extremism are not eligible for “conditional release” granted to those who sign the contract with the ministry of defence, to go to the war. Thus, Girkin can only sign an army contract if Vladimir Putin pardons him. Which will never happen — free and unhinged Girkin is a real threat to Putin’s regime, especially with a weapon in his hands. Plus he knows too much and would be a perfect witness for Putin’s Hague trial. And his worst offense, he insulted Putin personally — which makes Girkin a “traitor”, an unforgivable sin in the eyes of vengeful Putin. When his time of release gets near, Girkin will either “suddenly die” or get a new jail term — this time a much longer one. Girkin posted enough to be sentenced for “treason”, “discrediting the army” — or dozens of other offenses, designed by Putin’s regime to lock up the people who cause trouble. Girkin is finished. Anyone who is still supporting him might find themselves in FSB “interview rooms” pretty soon.

What are some positive aspects of Russian culture and its people? Russian military correspondents are furious: residents of Kursk region are evacuating, instead of queuing to sign up as volunteers for the Russian army. (Video in the comments below.) “What the heck??” barks a Russian man dressed in a military uniform. “As males, you should be defending your homes, you should be delivering food to our guys, or digging trenches — or if you can’t do it, just give your cars to our guys, so they can use them at the front. Why are you just driving away??” For 25 years, since Putin took helm in Russia, the state was training citizens to be passive: “They at the top know best what to do”, “we are just small people”, “we can’t change anything”. People have learned to don’t have any opinions of their own, because having an opinion can get you in trouble. They’ve learned to “stay out of politics”, learned to live by the motto, “my hut is at the edge of the village, I don’t know anything”. Putin’s administration chose to downplay “the situation in Kursk region” and Russian propagandists are now saying that “Ukraine made a foolish move” and “everything is under control, situation stabilized, no losses.” Kursk residents know it’s not true — they can look out of the window and see what happens, but because the state tells them “it’s all good”, they simply do what they feel is the right thing for them — run away. They don’t want to defend Putin’s regime, they don’t want to fight and possibly die defending their homeland. It’s weird, but there are no public protests in Russian towns taken over by the Ukrainian forces, as there were in spring 2022 when the Russian army invaded Ukrainian cities and thousands of Ukrainians went to town squares to protest against the Russian invaders — Ukrainian men, women, elders, kids were standing with bare hands against armed Russian soldiers, yelling at them, “Go home!!” “Occupiers, go home!” — protests in Kherson in March 2022. Similar mass protests were happening in many other Ukrainian towns captured by the Russian army. People in Kherson were standing with Ukrainian flags, with anti-Putin and anti-Russia posters, against armed Russians and military vehicles. Russians don’t protest. They seem to be indifferent to what is happening around them. They realized their officials lie to them — they knew it all along, but it was safer to pretend they believed them — and they have no idea what is real and what is not anymore, they just don’t trust anybody — but pretend to trust the guys who are in charge right now. If Ukrainians are in charge, they pretend to trust Ukrainians. If Russians are in charge, they pretend to trust Russians. Russian citizens have no opinions of their own — or if they do, they keep them buried so deep, they themselves are terrified to admit they have them. It’s not a “slave mentality” — it’s learned helplessness. They really think there is nothing they can do that will change anything. Obviously, this aspect of the modern Russian culture and collective psyche is highly beneficial to the advancing Ukrainian army, which doesn’t have to deal with hostile population. Rather, Ukrainians are dealing with passive, yet quietly curious population, compliant and eager to follow instructions. Russian State Duma member Vitaly Milonov called on men from the Kursk region to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense and defend their homeland on their own — obviously, Putin isn’t going to send to Kursk reinforcements from the front in Ukraine, where he’s sending most troops and equipment. Milonov, too, believes that only women, children and the elderly should be evacuating from Kursk, but local men should take on the defense of border areas. “No one has to do anything for Russian residents of border regions,” announced Milonov — they themselves must show that they can defend their land. With such an attitude from the Russian state, no wonder that Ukrainians keep taking over several more settlements every day. Isn’t it weird that Russians are willing to go to Ukraine “to make Russia great again” (and be paid “big wages”) — but have no desire or interest to defend their own homes?

When was slavery abolished in Russia? On July 1, 1966, workers of Soviet “collective farms” for the first time were paid salaries in actual money. Before that, Soviet peasants were de-facto slaves: In 1861, Emperor Alexander II signed the manifesto “On the most merciful granting to serfs of the rights of free rural inhabitants”, ending serfdom in Russia. But after the Bolshevik’s coup in October 1917 and the bloody civil war, communists brought back de-facto serfdom: they confiscated the farm land and animals from Russian peasants and locked them in “collective farms”. It’s only 50 years ago that the last Russian serfs were given the same rights as city workers (who also weren’t free in the USSR). Don’t believe the lies that marxists tell you about communism and socialism (in fact, when the Soviet communists failed to build communism for several decades, they simply named it “socialism” and told the masses that communism will follow soon). There had been no country in the history of the mankind that attempted to build a Marxist state and didn’t produce a totalitarian tyranny. Not even one.

The main dish on the menu was “Chicken Kyiv” cutlet. Yes, for real. Bizarrely, the “greatest country in the world” couldn’t find its own national dish to showcase for its esteemed guests. Frankly, I don’t even want to comment on it — there is just so much cynicism one can digest in a day. I’ll leave it to you.

Can you reverse Russian brainwashing? Top Russian propagandists are making millions — which they can only spend in Russia, because they all are sanctioned and their foreign assets are frozen. They forever bound themselves to Putin’s regime, and knowing the fate of Hitler’s propagandists, don’t have illusions about their future if Putin’s shady gamble in Ukraine fails. During the times of WWII, Goebbels’ propaganda machine was also pretty effective — even in America, some people were supporting Hitler’s ideas, while others insisted that America should mind its own business. 1941 protesters in America: “Why not peace with Hitler?” To counter Nazi propaganda, Walt Disney created a cartoon named “Der Fuehrer's face”, where Donald Duck is living a Nazi nightmare. It was designed to reverse the Nazi brainwashing. The cartoon was so successful, it won the Oscar for Best Animated Short Film at the 15th Academy Awards. In 1994, it was voted #22 of "The 50 Greatest Cartoons" of all time by members of the animation field. When the Nazi Germany was defeated in May 1945, the huge job of denazification of Germany began. Ending the Nazi propaganda was the start, debunking propaganda myths and revealing the truth were the next steps. The same job will be needed in Russia to reverse the brainwashing by Putin’s regime.

How does Putin think he will win against the rest of the world? This cover of “The Spectator” is dated October 2016. Putin has just increased 10 times the reach of Kremlin propaganda among western viewers, compared to the start of 2024 — and you can be sure they are not going to stop there. A network of pro-Kremlin bots, nicknamed Doppelgänger by western analysts, has sharply increased its reach among social media users in different countries, reported ‘The Insider’. This shocking fact was discovered by analysts of ‘AntibotNavalny’, who reviewed the reach of cleverly designed tweets, promoting Kremlin narratives. Analysts came to the conclusion that this level of coverage of the bot network was achieved thanks to texts generated by artificial intelligence. ‘Doppelgänger’ is a network of accounts disseminating Kremlin narratives aimed at Western audiences, including propaganda videos, caricatures of Western leaders, and links to “journalistic” articles from websites created by the Kremlin. Doppelgänger uses the same method as fraudulent websites that try to steal your money — only the Kremlin tries to steal your thoughts. So, Putin is massively escalating its hybrid war against the West. Russia is waging the war against the whole western civilization. For Putin, it’s the war for world domination. And every one of us is under attack.

Does Russophobia exist? Russophobia only exists in the vocabulary of Russian propagandists. In reality, people aren’t “irrationally terrified” of Russians or Russia — they have legitimate and absolutely rational fears of what actions a Russian person might undertake as an individual, while retaining ties with its motherland. Foreigners are also concerned about the constant threats against basically every country or state, leaders of which do not align themselves with Vladimir Putin and do not condone his war on Ukraine. The feeling towards Russians among most westerners isn’t of a “phobia”, but rather a contempt — people despise what Russian leaders are doing and what Russian people support and tolerate. The Russian propagandists should rather call it “Russocontempt” — this word describes the feeling more precisely.

Has Omsk oil refinery, Russia's largest oil refinery just caught fire and has blown up? Gazprom, local news. How much will this affect Russia's diesel, petrol, aviation and hydrofuels? How far is Umsk from Kiev? Is Palianytsia suspected? The explosion at the Omsk oil refinery yesterday was powerful — windows were blown out in nearby houses. According to Reuters, as a result of the explosion and subsequent fire at the Omsk oil refinery, the AVT-11 primary oil refining unit — most productive at the plant — was damaged and had to be shot down. That’s half of the plant's capacity. The fire area affected over 1,000 square meters. Omsk is about 3,000 km away from Ukraine and it’s unlikely the explosion was the result of a drone attack — although the new Ukrainian jet drone ‘Palianytsia’ can potentially fly that far, some experts believe. If Ukraine were able to hit this far (with a jet drone or another weapon), it would be a completely different reality that Russians would have to exist in.

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. The commander was pissed off about it: "I don't need this, now I have to do something for one more person." A day later the injured guy was already begging to die, realizing he wouldn’t survive. At the end, he bled to death. The dead were rarely pulled out from the field. It was too much trouble to even attempt it. Once Anton had to hide from a drone and crawled into an old dugout, and realized he was crawling on top of liquified bodies in uniform. The bodies were there for already 3–4 months. There was one guy in the unit of about 18–19, he was a draftee (all Russian men have to serve a 1-year compulsory military service, but the draftees are not supposed to be sent to Ukraine to the war). That guy was also tricked into signing a contract — in the military enlistment office where he arrived as a draftee, they simply gave him some papers to sign, and he signed, not realizing what it was. “A week and a half later, he was already at the front line,” says Anton. The guy’s family sent a letter, complaining to the prosecutor's office that he was forced to sign the contract. The battalion commander was furious about it and gave the order to “sort him out.” The teenage soldier was sent into an attack and killed within a week. Anton says his commander was constantly drunk. One day the commander ordered him to pick another drone from the headquarters — Anton argued it was unnecessary to do it at night, as they had a spare drone they could use, and at night it’s really easy to see a person on thermal visors. But the commander insisted. Anton managed to get to the headquarters, where they gave him a drone and a package “for the commander”. Anton looked inside the bag, and there were bottles of vodka and cognac. The commander sent him to get the alcohol for him and he didn’t care it was deadly dangerous. On the way back, Anton heard a drone over him and immediately an explosive dropped on him. Anton was wounded and couldn’t walk, but he realized he still had both his arms and legs. He threw away the bag with vodka and crawled into the nearest basement, got on the radio, said that he was wounded and asked for evacuation. They responded it was too dangerous to try to get him. After 20 minutes, he realized that he was bleeding out. “I was shaking all over, tremors, I definitely lost a liter of blood,” says Anton. He decided to crawl, and managed to make it to the line where he could be picked up — out of the firing range. Anton says that ”almost everyone drinks” at the front line — or they are using cheap drugs (“salts”). The commanders also steal strong pain killers from the first aid kits given to soldiers and use those. If a soldier refuses to follow orders, he isn’t sent to a military court for prosecution but simply shot by the commander’s underlings — his arms and legs are taped to a tree, and he’s shot at a point blank range. Sometimes a person may be dressed in 2 bulletproof vests and then shot at with a machine gun, his ribs get broken and he slowly dies. Or he’s shot at through a helmet — such shots take off the whole skull. Anton says that 2 soldiers in his unit were liquidated like this, for not following orders — they refused to go in an attack, because all previous groups were killed. Anton himself nearly got shot — when in the field, he noticed a drone in the sky and went back, but took to the left and ended up in a neighboring unit. That unit was looking for a mobilized soldier on the run and took Anton for the deserter. He was tied to a tree and about to be shot, there was a hole nearby, where 20–30 bodies were already lying. He was saved by a radio message that the runaway soldier was found. Do the Russian soldiers realize that Russia’s war in Ukraine is evil? Do they blame Putin for that? Nobody among the Russian troops at the front says things like "let's go overthrow Putin,” states Anton. “Of course, they say that he [Putin] has started some kind of screwup that no one needs.” ”Even the ‘patriots’ when they arrive, very soon start saying, ‘What are we even doing here, why the heck do we need this?’” “There are some ‘ultra patriots’, but they do not survive for long, because they are the first to run ahead and the first to get killed.” “There was this guy, 54 years old, his wife had cancer. He came not even for the money, but because he needed the benefits for a serviceman's family, so his wife could get the cancer treatment. He was saying: ‘I know that people get killed here, I made my choice. If I get killed, at least my wife will get 5 million ruble, she will get the treatment, the children will live well." That guy lived in a small regional town. His monthly salary was 35,000 ruble (about USD$400). He had 3 kids, his wife was sick. He saw it as his only option to help the wife and the kids. “You are not a human being there at all,” says Anton. He fears what is going to happen in Russia when all these people with the broken psyche come back. “When these people come back from the war with blood on their hands, with a broken psyche, who were in the same companies, detachments and so on, they will start to form groups, and these smaller groups will start to form bigger groups...” Anton says that plenty of weapons are transported back to Russia in bags with dead bodies — pulled into parts and hidden in these bags. An AK-47 costs about 40,000 ruble in Russia now ($460). Anton says that if the Russian soldiers are being utilized at the same rate as at his part of the front, Russia has suffered about 400,000 losses by now — killed and badly wounded. Anton says that no one signing an army contract should hope they’d come back with the money — because they won’t. At best, they can hope to come back home with the money in case of a serious wound — but then, “Do you want your mother to be wiping off your butt for the rest of your life?” “If you think there are some Nazis there... There are no Nazis, there are ordinary people. If you, so to say, go and kill your neighbor, would you be able to live with that for the rest of your life?” “This war is not worth it. This is not a war for the Fatherland, this is not a war for justice, not a war for freedom — this is a war for the complete bullshit. A war for the grandfather who is so crazy that he went and killed hundreds of thousands of people for nothing, just like that.” “You are not liberating anyone. He [the crazy grandfather] himself doesn't believe that he is liberating anyone, he doesn't give a f**k about all this — and even less about you.” What can the Russian men do to avoid being sent to the war? “Better run,” says Anton. ”No money? Take out loans and use that money to escape.” Anton himself deserted after getting wounded. Yesterday, Putin signed a decree raising the federal payout on signing the army contact to 400,000 rub. ($4,600) — it’s nearly twice as much as the state was paying before. Regions are also raising their payouts — St. Petersburg just raised it’s top-up to 1.8 million, and Moscow already lifted it to 1.9 million rub. ($22,000). Russia is running out of volunteers, so the prices for cannon fodder are rising. Putin is too scared to do another mobilization and force people to kill and die, because he knows how unpopular this war really is.

Do you know of any Russians who support Ukraine or are against Putin's actions in Eastern Europe? And how do you feel about the situation in the region? Singer Monetochka and rapper Noise MC are touring Europe with concerts, singing anti-war songs and donating money to Ukraine. As many other Russian creators who spoke openly against the war, they had to leave Russia after February 2022. 26-year-old Elizaveta ‘Liza’ Gyrdymova and 39-year-old Ivan Alekseyev collaborated for the first time 7 years ago on the song “Childfree”, depicting the desperation of ordinary Russians’ existence. In 2024, the Russian authorities intend to ban “the childfree ideology” as an extremist movement. Anyone who dares to speak openly about not wanting to make future soldiers for Putin’s army should be locked in prison! Videos of the duo’s songs are understandable with no translation and the message is powerful. (Videos in the comments below.) That’s why in Russia both Monetochka and Noise MC are labeled “foreign agents”. Basically, anyone who is well known in the Russian informational space and speaks against the war in Ukraine, is labeled a “foreign agent” by Putin’s regime. The law on “foreign agents” appeared in Russia in 2012, but since then it has been constantly updated, making it easier to proclaim any person or organization “a foreign agent”, thus effectively removing them from the Russian media and political space: those who cover activities of “foreign agents” (or work with them) risk getting the label of a “foreign agent” themselves. The bulk of “foreign agent” nominations occurred during the first 10 months of the war — when Russia’s ruling clique realized that their speedy “special military operation” is turning into a full-out positional war at 1000-km front that requires mobilization of all resources. There are also tens of thousands of Russians who got arrested for anti-war protests and posts, and were given fines or 10–15 days of administrative arrest, “to set them straight.” The vast majority of Russian citizens got the message — many emigrated after such arrests, and now support Ukraine from abroad. Regretfully, Putin’s regime was successful in turning most Russians who stayed in Russia into willing (or unwilling) accomplices of its genocidal war in Ukraine. By now, the civil anti-war protest in Russia has been thoroughly suppressed. Even defiant actions like attending the funeral of the leader of opposition Alexei Navalny, killed by Putin’s regime in February 2024 (attending a funeral is technically not against the law) can still create substantial consequences for the participants. 16 thousand people came to the funeral of Alexei Navalny in Moscow on March 1, 2024. Thousands more came to lay flowers in the following days. The FSB films such events and identifies the attendees, and then begins “working” on them. There are hundreds of thousands — possibly, millions — of people in Russia who who support Ukraine and are against Putin's actions in Eastern Europe. They are just saying nothing. But even those who show support for the war — as required by the state — aren’t going to be upset if the war ends tomorrow, and they don’t care about “Russia’s victory” — as the Soviet people didn’t care about “the USSR victory” when a withdrawal of the Soviet troops from Afghanistan was announced in 1989, after a 10-year “international duty mission”. 1989: Withdrawal of the Soviet troops from Afghanistan. Literally, if Putin died today and his successor announced that Russia is withdrawing troops from Ukraine, the vast majority of Russians would breathe a huge sigh of relief. Everyone in Russia is tired of this war. Even the guy who started it all.

What is your analysis of the satellite images of the Ukrainian Defence Intelligence drone strikes on the Russian radar station in Orenburg Oblast? On May 26, a long-range Ukrainian drone attacked an over-the-horizon radar station in Russia in Orenburg region — at a distance of more than 1,800 km. Orsk is located 140 km further from the front line in Ukraine than the Bashkir city of Salavat, which was previously the furthest location from Ukraine attacked by Ukrainian drones in Russia. The drone targeted the Voronezh-M missile attack warning radar station in the village of Gorkovskoye near the town of Orsk in Orenburg region. The station is fairly new — it was commissioned in 2017. 2 days ago, Ukraine already hit another Voronezh-DM radar station, located in the Krasnodar Territory. “Voronezh” type stations are designed to detect and track ballistic and cruise missiles and other aerodynamic objects at distances up to 6,000 These long-range radar stations are part of Russia’s “strategic umbrella”. Since 2011, these radar stations became part of Russia’s Aerospace Defense Forces. It is these stations that Russia is using to hit targets in Ukraine. Like the attack on Kharkiv hypermarket last Saturday.

Is there running inflation currently in Russia? How are people coping with it? Residents of regional Russian towns are the first to experience the mighty hit of running inflation. On July 26, 2024, Russia raised the base rate to 18.00% per annum. The central bank of Russia explained that “inflation has accelerated and is significantly higher than the April 2024 forecast,” but talks about the need to raise the base rate had been ongoing for months — the rate was kelp at “low” 26% per annum to allow for Putin’s re-election and inauguration. Life has become more expensive in Russia within the last year: At the same time, there is nearly no money for increases in wages in the state budget — all money goes to war. With the running inflation, interest rates for home loans in Russia are over 20%. Russia is turning into a giant Ponzi scheme that’s doomed to collapse.

Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the media that weapons from the United States and other Western countries supplied to Ukraine are already hitting targets in Russia. “We proceed from the fact that American and other Western weapons are hitting targets on Russian territory,” said Lavrov. Great point Lavrov! If Russia thinks this, then clearly it’s not a problem. No “red lines” whatsoever. Great job Lavrov.

What is wrong with the Russian government? 46-year-old son of Sergei Mironov, leader of the party “A Just Russia — For Truth”, left Russia and broke off relations with his father, because he is against the war. ”When my father yells in the State Duma about the Nazis in Ukraine, I feel personally responsible,” said Mironov-junior, who was born in 1978. Why does Russia refuse to accept equal blame for the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and the start of WWII? On August 23, 1939, two criminal regimes — organizers of World War 2, Germany and the Soviet Union, signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and its secret protocol, defining the split of European territories between them. The pact gave the final impetus to the new world war, which began just 8 days later, with Germany’s attack on Poland. Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact: German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop (left), Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and USSR Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov (right) on August 23, 1939 in the Kremlin after signing the pact. Stalin made a toast after the ceremony: "I know how much the German people love their Fuhrer. Therefore, I want to drink to his health." On September 1, 1939 Germany’s attacked Poland. The Soviet Union attacked Poland on September 17, 1939. On September 22, Nazis and Soviets held a joint parade in Brest, celebrating their victory. For 50 years, the USSR leaders denied that there was a secret appendix to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. In 1946, at the Nuremberg Trials, the former State Secretary of the German Foreign Ministry, Ernst von Weizsäcker, spoke about the existence of a secret additional protocol between the USSR and Germany. This was confirmed by other defendants, and one of the lawyers even wanted to read the text of this protocol, but he was not allowed: the USSR representatives called it a fake and said such a document never existed. In 1948, the secret protocol, based on photocopies of the German original that had not survived, was published in the US State Department collection "Nazi-Soviet Relations. 1939-1941". It also included the correspondence between Nazi and Soviet diplomats, which contained references to secret agreements. But the Soviet Union continued to claim that this was a falsification, that no additional secret appendix to the 1939 agreements ("On Non-Aggression" and "On Friendship and Borders") between the USSR and Germany existed. Moreover: in response to the publication by the State Department, Moscow published its own work titled "Falsifiers of History". But it did not contain a single complete copy of a document, only a few fragments. Stalin didn’t want to be blamed in starting the World War with Hitler, and used the status of the USSR as one of the “victors of WW2” to suppress this extremely important information. Molotov, who signed the non-aggression pact and the secret protocol to it, denied its existence until his death in 1986. Minister of Foreign Affairs of the USSR Vyacheslav Molotov in Berlin, November 14, 1940. It was hard to prove that such a document existed: one party that signed it (Hitler's Germany) no longer existed, and the other (the Soviet Union) denied that it existed at all, and had no intention of publishing it. Only in 1989, the Soviet leaders admitted that such secret protocol existed, on request of representatives of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. A copy of the German document was published in the USSR. The actual copy of the secret protocol in Russian was first kept in Stalin's safe and then in the archive of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. In 1992, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the archive of the Communist Party was declassified and the secret protocol was discovered. From that moment, the existence of a secret additional treaty to the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact had become a reliably recognized fact not only in the West, not only in the Baltic countries, Moldova and Ukraine, but also in Russia itself. But now, Putin’s propaganda downplays the importance of the secret agreement between Hitler and Stalin how they would divide Europe, and overemphasizes that it was a non-aggression pact, which allowed the USSR 2 more years without the war. Completely disregarding the fact that without the secret agreement to split European lands, there possibly wouldn’t happen such a war. Putin went much further than Stalin — he now claims it was Russia that defeated Hitler (not even the USSR but Russia), and the whole world must be grateful to Russia for defeating the Nazi regime. Putin’s propaganda promoted this idea for years, having convinced some westerners that Russia was some kind of “savior” nation. And then Putin used this notion to attack Ukraine: he labeled Ukrainians “Nazis” and sent the Russian troops to invade Ukraine “to defeat a Neo-Nazi regime”. Putin hoped it would work and the world would buy into it. He still hopes he can convince us.

How does the arrest of Laurent Vinatier, a French researcher who was charged with violating the "foreign agents" law in Russia, affect international relations? Yesterday, he appeared in a Moscow court for a hearing, asking to be allowed to stay under house arrest, but his request was denied by the judge. Vinatier seemed a shadow of his confident self from a month ago. He appeared at the hearing via a video link. The French consul general in Moscow was present at the hearing. Vinatier was arrested immediately after the French president Macron said that France would send troops to Ukraine, in the worst Russia’s traditions of “hostage diplomacy”. About the same time 26-year-old native of Donbas with dual Russian and Ukrainian citizenship was detained in France on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack. At the very first hearing on June 7 that sent him to jail on accusations of failing to register as a “foreign agent”, Vinatier was demonstratively thrown in a cage in the courtroom. At the hearing on July 4, the prosecution alleged that Vinatier was guilty of collecting military information. The prosecution didn’t disclose what information Vinatier shouldn’t be privy to, but stated that it "could be used against state security." The accusation of not registering as a “foreign agent” — which Vinatier said he wasn’t aware he was required to do — is usually reserved for Russian citizens who are financed by foreign entities and involved in political activities. But recent changes to the law require anyone who “collects information on military issues” to register as a “foreign agent”. The 48-year-old Frenchman is an adviser with the Geneva-based ‘Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue’, a Swiss conflict mediation organization, and a long-time researcher of Russia and other post-Soviet countries. Russia has been using its "foreign agent" laws to jail domestic critics for a long time, and now the regime is doing it to foreign citizens as well. On June 21, 2024, Vinatier was included in the Russian register of “foreign agents”. Vinatier attended the court hearing on July 4 via a video link from the detention centre — he wasn’t brought to the court. The judge extended his detention until August 5. Any foreign citizen in Russia is a potential hostage and an instrument of exerting pressure on democratically elected governments, especially during elections. Hostages are also used as leverage in negotiations. Kremlin bots are pushing such topics in social media to stir emotions and cause division. In case of Vinatier, Kremlin bots are already driving the story to notoriety. Under the current accusation, Vinatier can be imprisoned for up to 5 years.

Did Ukraine just test its first ballistic missile? Ukraine had the capability to build ballistic missiles since the times of the USSR, but after signing the Budapest memorandum in 1994, Ukraine had to dispose of its arsenal of carriers of strategic nuclear warheads. Ukraine also surrendered to Russia many missiles that Putin’s army used in attacks since February 2022. So, when president Zelenskyy announced on August 27, 2024, that Ukraine has successfully tested its new ballistic missile, it was something that many analysts expected for a long time. Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon (left), who was a friend of former Ukrainian president Leonid Kuchma (right) described their conversation in 2006 when Kuchma told him that Ukraine had both the capability and expertise to build ballistic missiles. Kuchma also told Gordon that Ukraine was able to build “as many as necessary” ballistic missiles. Leonid Kuchma knew what he was talking about. He began working on ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant in the Ukrainian city of Dnipropetrovsk in 1960, straight after graduation from a university as an engineer. On ‘Yuzhmash’, Kuchma was working in the design bureau, where the Soviet missile systems were created. Then he moved to the position of technical director of rocket tests at the Baikonur Cosmodrome — the #1 space rocket launching pad of the USSR. During his career, Kuchma worked as a chief of both legendary flagships of the Ukrainian rocket and space industry — ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant and ‘Yuzhnoye’ design bureau. For his contribution to development of rocket engineering, Kuchma was awarded the Lenin Prize in 1979 (12 years before the dissolution of the USSR). After Kuchma became the 2nd president of independent Ukraine, the first Ukrainian satellite "Sich-1" was launched into space (1995). In an interview to BBC in June 2022, Kuchma said that the latest developments of Dnepropetrovsk aerospace engineers included analogues of western weapons that Ukraine had to beg western partners for: for example, missile systems with a range of hundreds of kilometers. So, the appearance of Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles was only a matter of time — and I think Putin knew it, this is why he was in such a hurry to pressure Ukraine to sign a “peace agreement” that would prohibit further development of Ukrainian weapons. But Putin underestimated both Ukraine and the West. And now his strategic loss is obvious to anyone keeping abreast of the latest developments in this war.

Can Russian soldiers refuse orders? Sometimes the handcuffs were nailed to a tree, so the person couldn’t even sit down. The commanders told the brothers that they would anyway be sent to an assault, but if they didn’t agree to fight, they would be pushed on the battlefield with no support, to a certain death. The brothers were also separated and assigned to different units. Once, Semyon managed to film a video of how a man in his unit was being tied to a tree. Very quickly after that, he was called to the commander and forced to withdraw the application that he made to the military prosecutor's office and delete his posts. The last thing Semyon managed to tell his family was that the commanders threatened him that he would also be tied to a tree, or transferred to the unit of kamikaze stormtroopers. After that, both brothers disappeared. Only recently did the family learn that Semyon was killed, apparently around the same time, in December 2023. The place and circumstances of his death are unknown. His body was delivered in a closed coffin, and the family was forbidden to open it. The state said he was identified by the DNA, supplied by his mother, and his body tag. The coffin was delivered to the family in August 2024. What happened to his brother Gennady is unknown. Most likely, he perished in pointless “meat attacks” or in one of the many "pits" where commanders throw ”refuseniks”. Extrajudicial punishments in the Russian army are now perceived as a norm. The Russian state does not react in any way to complaints of soldiers about their commanders. Soldiers in the Russian army are viewed and treated worse than slaves — especially the mobilized (as compared to volunteers on a contract). The Russian military and the office of prosecutor refused to investigate the circumstances of death and disappearance of the brothers. No matter what the families of the forcibly mobilized soldiers do and which government bodies they try to appeal to, their loved ones end up either in a “pit” on the occupied Ukrainian territory or dead. Once the army has you in its claws, there is no way out. The whole Russian army is one giant war crime machine. And the torture engine is what keeps it going.

How high are Russian salaries in general? According to Russian statistics, the average monthly salary (after tax) in Russia is USD $648. It’s lower than in Mexico, but higher than in India. How many peoples in Baltic countries were killed because of the Soviet deportation? On June 14, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia commemorate the day of victims of communist terror, mass Soviet deportations in 1941. There were 2 types of deportees: regular people who were shipped off to Siberia, often whole families, and political prisoners. Political prisoners were those who actively resisted the Soviet occupation. They were sent to concentration camps (GULAG). Often charges were made up and people were sent to GULAG just to make the numbers, as required by the NKVD plan on “ideological cleanup”. No one was safe. Many families were taken just to fill the quotas if the listed family couldn’t be found; others were taken because they had similar names to those listed. Mass deportations provided the USSR with slave labour in underpopulated parts of its empire, but the main goal was to transform the Baltic countries from proudly independent, functioning states into permanently subservient provinces. 2 years earlier, in 1939, the Soviets and Nazis formed an alliance by agreeing in their Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact to illegally divide the European states between them through crimes of aggression, thus igniting the World War 2. Obviously, this was all totally illegal under international and domestic laws of these countries. After liquidating politicians, the first wave of mass deportations in June 1941 aimed to decapitate the independent states. Only those deemed “redeemable” (i.e. those who were innocent) were deported. Stalin’s ideology always was, “no person — no problem.” Living conditions in Siberia were extremely harsh, whichever group of deportees people belonged to. People were simply dropped off the train in the middle of nowhere, and had to build houses and find food by themselves. That is, if you even survived the journey. Many did not. Baltic people were always mostly agricultural nations, and had an extremely strong connection to their land, going back to the Baltic pagan religion, many elements of which are still part of the Baltic identity. Soviet deportations tore the very fabric of this identity. June 1941 deportations were conducted simultaneously across large parts of Eastern Europe, not only in Baltics. And deportations continued after the WW2. In total, over the years, the Soviets subjected an estimated 6 million people under their rule to forced migration. The Russification of occupied territories of Ukraine that we see today is an old Russian tradition, going back to the USSR and the Russian empire. Mass killings and deportation of people and bringing Russians to replace them is something Russia has never been made to answer for. In 2021 Putin ordered to close ‘Memorial’, the oldest human rights organization in Russia and a Nobel peace prize winner. Founded in late 1980s, its goal was to document political repressions in the Soviet Union and build a database of victims of the Great Terror and GULAG camps. Once again, Russians are supposed to forget the past and erase from memory all the crimes their ancestors participated in. Then, crimes against humanity and genocide can be committed without a single pang of conscience. We are seeing it now. Again. But just as Russian imperialism failed in the Baltics, despite (or because of) mass deportations, we know it will fail again against Ukraine.

Finland before the war with the Soviets. For a long time, regiments of the Red Army were concentrating around the border with Finland, engaging in all types of vile provocations. Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim (1867–1951) charted the course of Finnish history and was voted greatest Finn of all time. He served in the Russian Imperial Army for decades, and later became a war hero in his home country of Finland. He was the symbol of the Finnish struggle against Soviet Russia during the Winter War of 1939–1940. The Soviet plan to take over Finland was touted as “help to the brotherly Finnish nation”. For that, the fictitious “People's Republic of Finland” was created in the Kremlin, as opposition to the “Helsinki Junta”. The photo shows destruction from Soviet bombs on Frederiksgatan Street. Later, when footage of burning Helsinki spread all over the world, the Soviets began to lie that they bombed “only military targets,” but in fact, most of the bombs fell in the city center — around the central train station and major streets. Stalin's tactics of “not a step back” with barrier troops behind the storm regiments were first used in the Finnish war (the task of “barrier troops” was to shoot anyone trying to retreat). The photo shows Red Army soldiers frozen in a trench: the soldiers were simply left to freeze in the forest. Red Army soldiers captured by Finns. One of the notable operations was the battle on the Raat road, in which the Finns defeated the 44th division of the Soviets. A considerable part of the dead soldiers were Ukrainians and Belarusians, whom the Soviets mobilized to fight against Finns — although the Finns did nothing wrong to Ukrainians and Belarusians. Stalin asked for negotiations and signed a “peace deal” with the Finns. Britain and France had considered providing the Finns with military assistance, but they took too long to actually deliver any. Still, one of the reasons why Stalin offered the peace deal to Finland was his worry to be faced with a war against France and Britain. Stalin planned to use the 1940 Peace Treaty (which emasculated Finnish defensive lines) as an interim break, followed by a renewed attack — once the threat of the Western intervention was over. The cost to Finland was the loss of 11% of its territory — in fact, Stalin demanded more land than the Red Army managed to occupy. 410,000 Finns living on the territories that were being transferred to the USSR (12% of the population of Finland at the time) had to leave their houses and evacuate to the regions that Finland managed to save, because they didn’t wish to live under the Soviet rule. Almost the whole population of the ceded territories chose to relocate. Stalin didn’t object the people leaving, but demanded that the buildings and machinery were left behind intact. The war lasted 105 days — 3.5 months. The “peace deal” was signed in March 1940. In just 3 months, in June 1940, Stalin invaded and annexed 3 Baltic countries — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. For the next 50 years, the Baltics had to live under the Soviet occupation, undergo extensive Russification, had to send their men to the Soviet army — including during the period of the USSR invasion of Afghanistan. Meanwhile, the Finns had built one of the richest and happiest countries on Earth.
